CASE PUD 2026-000031 ENTRY NO. 119 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 08/31/2026 - PAGE 1 OF 4




           BEFORE THE CORPORATION COMMISSION OF THE STATE OF OKLAHOMA

          IN THE MATTER OF THE APPLICATION OF                       )
          OKLAHOMA GAS AND ELECTRIC COMPANY                         ) Case No. PUD2026-000031
          FOR COMMISSION APPROVAL OF ELECTRIC                       )
          SERVICE AGREEMENTS AND PREAPPROVAL                        )
          OF CAPACITY PURCHASE AGREEMENTS                           )
          PURSUANT TO 17 O.S. § 286(C)                              )

                       Redacted Confidential Testimony Summary of Kimber L. Shoop

         Direct Testimony

                In his Direct Testimony, Kimber Shoop first provided his educational qualifications and
         employment history. He is the Director of Regulatory Affairs for Oklahoma Gas and Electric
         Company (“OG&E”). The overall purpose of his testimony is to support the Company’s request
         for Commission approval of three Electric Service Agreements (“ESAs”) with Google, which
         became effective               , and to seek pre-approval of two Capacity Purchase Agreements
         (“CPAs”) under which Google will sell OG&E needed generation capacity from two solar farms
         within OG&E’s service territory.

                 Mr. Shoop testified that Google is developing three data center sites that will add
         significant demand to OG&E’s system beginning in 2026, ramping to over                 in 2028 and
         then to over            by 2036. He stated that OG&E and Google worked together to develop
         unique terms and conditions that ensure the Company will be able to recover the costs of the large
         investments needed to serve Google while protecting OG&E’s other customer classes from any
         potential rate impacts. He explained that existing system costs will be spread over many more
         kilowatt-hours, resulting in all retail customers on the system paying less per kilowatt-hour, and
         that the new load puts downward pressure on rates for everyone. He further testified that customer
         protections negotiated in the special contracts include large contribution in aid of construction
         payments totaling over               , significant performance security, long-term commitment from
         Google with exit fees, minimum demand and energy charges, and recognition that any potential
         adverse rate impact to other customer classes will be reviewed and addressed in each general rate
         proceeding. He noted that OG&E is also developing a Large Load Tariff that will propose pricing
         that protects existing customers beyond the protections contained in the ESAs.

                Mr. Shoop then testified regarding OG&E’s significant capacity needs, explaining that the
         Company’s 2024 Integrated Resource Plan showed a significant capacity need that has only grown.
         He presented data showing that the summer capacity need under the 2025 IRP Update is 1,083
         MW in 2028, growing to 2,223 MW in 2031. He stated that even after all projects contracted from
         the 2024 All Source RFP are placed in service, OG&E still has significant needs in both summer
         and winter, with the summer need at 976 MW in 2028 alone, growing to nearly 2,800 MW in 2034,
         and the winter need at almost 1,200 MW in 2028, growing to over 3,000 MW in 2034. He
         explained that the two CPAs will not completely satisfy the Company’s capacity needs but will
         provide approximately 360 MW of accredited summer capacity and 120 MW of accredited winter

         capacity from two solar facilities: Rush Springs at 200 MW expected in service spring 2027 and
         High Spring at 400 MW expected in service spring 2028.

                 Mr. Shoop explained that the CPAs are beneficial for customers because the cost for each
         CPA is fixed over the 15-year term at                                   , and this price is roughly
         26% lower than the lowest-cost bid initially offered into the Company’s 2024 All Source RFP and
         approximately 58% lower than the least-cost CPA the Company ultimately executed through the
         RFP. He stated that the CPAs also include protections such as firm delivery obligations and
         alternative-facility nomination options to ensure capacity is available when needed, and that the
         Company will only pay for the amount of capacity that is actually scheduled and received. He
         noted that the CPAs contain provisions requiring Google to identify and provide capacity from
         alternative facilities at no additional cost under certain conditions.

                 Mr. Shoop concluded by testifying that OG&E requests the Commission approve the three
         special contracts with Google and grant pre-approval of the two CPAs pursuant to 17 O.S. Section
         286(C), including a determination that OG&E has a need for the capacity provided by these CPAs
         and that the CPAs are reasonable compared to the All-Source RFP bids. He stated that OG&E
         requests authorization to recover the costs of the CPAs through its Fuel Adjustment Clause,
         consistent with the recovery directed by the Commission in Order No. 753440 in Case No. PUD
         2025-000038. He further testified that OG&E requests approval from the Commission by October
         30, 2026, explaining that if the long-term agreements are not approved by that date, the negotiated
         customer protections will not apply until the Commission issues an order and the Special Contract
         is fully in effect, and that timely approval will ensure that OG&E’s existing customers remain
         protected.

         Rebuttal Testimony

                In his Rebuttal Testimony, Mr. Shoop explained the purpose of his testimony is to
         summarize the case up to this point and to respond to several arguments raised in Responsive
         Testimony, particularly regarding OG&E’s compliance with the pre-approval statute, the
         consideration of reasonable alternatives, the failsafe provision in the Google Electric Service
         Agreements, and his final recommendations to the Commission.

                 Mr. Shoop testified regarding 17 O.S. Section 286(C), the pre-approval statute, explaining
         that it allows rate-regulated electric companies like OG&E to seek Commission approval to
         construct or purchase electric generating facilities or enter into long-term contracts for purchased
         power and capacity. He stated that the statute requires OG&E to demonstrate a need for the facility
         and that, if need is established, the facility is considered used and useful and subject to cost
         recovery. He further noted that the statute requires the Commission to enter an order after
         consideration of reasonable alternatives. He testified that OG&E has complied with the
         requirements of the statute, establishing a need for new generating capacity through its Integrated
         Resource Plans, a need that no party in the proceeding disputes, and that OG&E considered
         reasonable alternatives as testified by OG&E witness Schuermann. He therefore recommended
         approval of the Rush Springs and High Spring Capacity Purchase Agreements.

                 Mr. Shoop then testified in response to PUD witness Givens, who raised questions about
         the consideration of reasonable alternatives because the CPAs were not bid into an RFP. He stated
         that nothing in the pre-approval statute or OCC rules requires a capacity resource to be bid into an
         RFP to demonstrate that reasonable alternatives have been considered. He explained that the
         Legislature clearly knows how to mandate competitive solicitations, as it did in Section 286(C)(7)
         for natural gas transportation contracts, and that the Commission’s implementing rules expressly
         contemplate situations where the competitive bidding RFP process is not utilized. He testified that
         OG&E recently conducted an RFP and assessed the market for new generation capacity, then
         compared the CPAs to that recent RFP, which constitutes clear and timely evidence of available
         market alternatives. He further noted that a recent amendment to the pre-approval statute, Section
         286(C)(2), specifically provides that bids received through a competitive bidding process within
         twelve months following the final bid due date shall be considered substantial evidence to satisfy
         the consideration of reasonable alternatives. He confirmed that OG&E received bids in its 2024
         All Source RFP on September 25, 2024, and that final pricing for the CPAs was established on
         September 12, 2025, well within the twelve-month window. He also rejected PUD’s suggestion
         that the Commission should set an intentionally high bar to discourage utilities from evading RFP
         requirements, stating that there are no RFP requirements being evaded and that the test for
         prudence should remain whether the project is fair, just, reasonable, and in the public interest.

                 Mr. Shoop also addressed the failsafe provision identified in the Google Electric Service
         Agreements. He noted that PUD and AG witnesses proposed specific details about how the failsafe
         provision should operate, including PUD Witness Givens recommending an annual with-and-
         without Google analysis and AG Witness Beling outlining specific details for that analysis. He
         stated that OG&E has proposed a Customer Class Protection Charge in the XLPL Tariff proceeding
         in Case No. PUD2026-00046 to embody the failsafe concept, and that the details of the with-and-
         without analysis will be decided by the Commission in a general rate case following the addition
         of the XLPL load to the system. He testified that it is premature for the Commission to determine
         precisely how that analysis should be done until it has all relevant facts and circumstances.

                 Mr. Shoop concluded by recommending that the Commission grant approval of OG&E’s
         three Electric Service Agreements with Google and pre-approval of the two CPAs pursuant to 17
         O.S. Section 286(C). He requested that the Commission determine that OG&E has a need for the
         capacity provided by the CPAs and that the CPAs are reasonable compared to the All-Source RFP
         bids, representing the lowest reasonable cost options for meeting OG&E’s current resource
         capacity needs. He also requested that the Commission authorize OG&E to recover the costs of
         the CPAs through its FCA, similar to the recovery granted in Case No. PUD2025-000038. He
         stated that the record demonstrates OG&E has a capacity need, has considered reasonable
         alternatives, and has negotiated customer protections that multiple responsive witnesses
         acknowledge are substantial and effective, and that remaining disputes largely involve future rate
         design and regulatory frameworks to be addressed in future rate cases.
